paper.title: Dose-response of iron supplementation on fatigue

paper_doc.title: Dose-response of iron supplementation on fatigue
paper_doc.authors: Park, J.¹, Singh, R.²  ·  ¹ Department of Clinical Nutrition, Fake University Hospital  ·  ² School of Public Health, Fake Institute of Health Sciences
paper_doc.abstract: Background: Fatigue is the most frequent complaint of adults with iron deficiency without anaemia, yet the amount of oral iron needed to relieve it is not settled. Most trials compare a single dose against placebo, which says little about how much iron is enough. Methods: We conducted a 12-week, double-blind, randomised trial in 150 iron-deficient, non-anaemic adults aged 18 to 55 years, allocated in equal numbers to 20, 40 or 60 mg of elemental iron daily. The primary outcome was the change in a validated fatigue score from baseline to week 12, modelled as a linear function of the daily dose. Secondary outcomes were serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, haemoglobin, adherence and gastrointestinal adverse events. Results: In 150 iron-deficient adults, fatigue scores fell with increasing iron dose. Ferritin rose in every arm and most in the highest-dose arm, while gastrointestinal complaints were more frequent at 60 mg. The estimated dose-response slope and its confidence interval are reported in the Results. Conclusions: Within the range studied, larger daily doses of oral iron produced larger reductions in fatigue, at the cost of more gastrointestinal complaints. Clinicians may weigh these two effects when choosing a dose.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide and affects a large share of otherwise healthy adults, in particular women of reproductive age, frequent blood donors, vegetarians and people who train for endurance sports. In its early stage, iron stores are depleted while haemoglobin remains within the normal range. This state, iron deficiency without anaemia, is often missed because routine blood counts look normal, and its symptoms are non-specific.
Fatigue is the symptom that brings most of these patients to a clinician. Iron is needed not only for haemoglobin but for myoglobin, for the cytochromes of the respiratory chain and for several enzymes of neurotransmitter synthesis, so a shortage could plausibly cause tiredness before any anaemia appears. Several randomised trials have found that iron given to non-anaemic women with low ferritin reduces self-reported fatigue compared with placebo, and systematic reviews have reached similar conclusions, while noting that the trials were small and used different doses, formulations and fatigue scales.
What these trials cannot answer is how the benefit depends on dose. Clinical guidelines recommend daily doses that vary several-fold, from about 20 mg to more than 100 mg of elemental iron, and higher doses are known to cause more nausea, constipation and abdominal pain, which in turn lower adherence. Studies of iron absorption suggest that a large single dose raises circulating hepcidin and reduces the fraction of iron absorbed from the next dose, so the extra iron in a high dose may be partly wasted. If the effect on fatigue levels off at modest doses, patients could be spared the side effects of high doses with no loss of benefit.
We therefore designed a trial that randomised iron-deficient, non-anaemic adults to three daily doses of the same oral iron preparation and estimated the change in fatigue per unit of dose. Our primary hypothesis was that the reduction in fatigue would increase with dose across the range studied. Our secondary aims were to describe the corresponding changes in iron status and the frequency of adverse events at each dose.

sections.heading: 2. Methods
sections.text:
2.1 Study design and setting
The trial was a single-centre, parallel-group, double-blind, randomised dose-comparison trial carried out at the outpatient nutrition clinic of Fake University Hospital. The protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee and registered before the first participant was enrolled. All participants gave written informed consent. The trial followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and is reported according to the CONSORT statement for randomised trials.
2.2 Participants
Adults aged 18 to 55 years who reported fatigue for at least four weeks were screened. Eligible participants had a serum ferritin below 30 µg/L, a haemoglobin within the sex-specific reference range and a baseline fatigue score of at least 10 on the scale described below. We excluded people with a known cause of fatigue other than iron deficiency, including thyroid disease, depression under treatment, sleep apnoea and chronic inflammatory disease; people with a C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L; pregnant or breastfeeding women; and anyone who had taken iron supplements or received an iron infusion in the previous three months.
2.3 Randomisation and blinding
Participants were randomised in a 1:1:1 ratio to 20, 40 or 60 mg of elemental iron daily, using computer-generated permuted blocks of six stratified by sex. The allocation list was prepared by a statistician not involved in recruitment and held by the hospital pharmacy. All capsules were identical in size, colour and weight, and each participant took three capsules each morning, containing iron sulphate or an inert filler in the proportions needed for the allocated dose. Participants, clinic staff and outcome assessors were unaware of the allocation until the database was locked.
2.4 Intervention
The capsules were taken on an empty stomach with water for 12 weeks. Participants were advised to avoid tea, coffee and calcium-rich foods for one hour after the dose. Adherence was assessed by capsule counts at weeks 4, 8 and 12 and expressed as the percentage of the prescribed capsules taken.

sections.heading: 2.5 Outcomes
sections.text:
The primary outcome was the change in fatigue from baseline to week 12, measured with the Fatigue Severity Index, a 30-point self-report scale on which higher scores mean more fatigue. The index has been validated in adult outpatients and has good internal consistency and test-retest reliability. Participants completed it at baseline and at weeks 4, 8 and 12, without access to their earlier answers.
Secondary outcomes were serum ferritin, transferrin saturation and haemoglobin at baseline and week 12, measured in fasting morning samples in the hospital laboratory; adherence; and adverse events. Adverse events were recorded at every visit with a structured checklist of gastrointestinal symptoms followed by an open question.
2.6 Sample size
The trial was designed to estimate the dose-response slope with useful precision rather than to test a difference between two arms. Based on the variability of fatigue change in earlier trials, 50 participants per arm were expected to give a confidence interval for the slope narrow enough to distinguish a clinically relevant effect from none, allowing for up to 10% loss to follow-up.
2.7 Statistical analysis
Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle and included all randomised participants. The change in the fatigue score was analysed with a linear mixed model with participant as a random effect, daily dose as a continuous fixed effect, visit as a categorical fixed effect, and baseline fatigue score and sex as covariates. The dose-response slope was expressed as the reduction in fatigue score per 10 mg of daily iron, with a 95% confidence interval. Missing outcomes were handled by the mixed model under the assumption that data were missing at random; a sensitivity analysis used multiple imputation. Departure from linearity was examined by adding a quadratic term for dose. Secondary outcomes were compared between arms with analysis of covariance adjusted for the baseline value. All analyses were done with standard statistical software and a two-sided significance level of 5%.

sections.heading: 3. Results
sections.text:
3.1 Participants
Of 412 adults screened, 150 were eligible and were randomised, 50 to each arm. Recruitment took place over 14 months. The most common reasons for exclusion were a ferritin above the threshold, anaemia and a raised C-reactive protein. In total, 144 participants completed the 12-week visit; the six who did not were lost to follow-up or withdrew for reasons unrelated to the study capsules in four cases and because of gastrointestinal complaints in two. The three arms were similar at baseline in age, sex, body mass index, iron status and fatigue score (Table 2).

figure.caption: Figure 1. Flow of participants through the trial: screening, randomisation to 20, 40 or 60 mg of elemental iron daily, follow-up and analysis.

table.caption: Table 2. Baseline characteristics of the randomised participants by arm (mean or number)

sections.heading: 3.2 Iron status
sections.text: Serum ferritin rose in all three arms over the 12 weeks, and the rise was larger with higher doses. Transferrin saturation followed the same pattern. Haemoglobin, which was normal at baseline, changed little in any arm. The proportion of participants whose ferritin reached at least 30 µg/L by week 12 increased from the low-dose arm to the high-dose arm (Table 4). The increase in ferritin per extra 10 mg of iron was smaller between 40 and 60 mg than between 20 and 40 mg, which is consistent with reduced fractional absorption at higher doses.

figure.caption: Figure 2. Mean serum ferritin at baseline and week 12 in each arm. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals.

sections.heading: 3.3 Fatigue
sections.text: Fatigue scores fell in all three arms during the trial, with most of the fall occurring in the first eight weeks. The reduction at week 12 was larger in the higher-dose arms. In the linear mixed model, the reduction in fatigue increased steadily with the daily dose of iron. Table 3 gives the dose-response slope: 0.45 points per 10 mg (95% CI 0.30 to 0.60). Adding a quadratic term for dose did not improve the fit of the model, so there was no evidence that the effect levelled off within the range studied. The multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis gave a similar estimate. The slope was similar in women and men, although the number of men was small.

table.caption: Table 3. Dose-response of the change in Fatigue Severity Index from baseline to week 12 (linear mixed model, intention to treat, n = 150)
rows: Dose-response slope, points per 10 mg of daily iron

figure.caption: Figure 3. Mean Fatigue Severity Index at baseline and at weeks 4, 8 and 12 in each arm. Lower scores mean less fatigue.

sections.heading: 3.4 Adherence and adverse events
sections.text: Adherence by capsule count was high in all arms but slightly lower in the 60 mg arm. Gastrointestinal adverse events were reported by more participants as the dose increased; the most frequent were nausea, constipation and dark stools. No serious adverse events occurred, and two participants in the 60 mg arm stopped taking the capsules because of abdominal discomfort.

table.caption: Table 4. Iron status at week 12, adherence and adverse events by arm
rows: Stopped capsules because of adverse events, n

sections.heading: 4. Discussion
sections.text:
In this randomised trial in non-anaemic adults with iron deficiency, the reduction in fatigue over 12 weeks grew with the daily dose of oral iron across the range of 20 to 60 mg, with no sign that the benefit levelled off. At the same time, gastrointestinal complaints became more frequent and adherence slightly lower as the dose increased.
Our findings agree with earlier placebo-controlled trials that found less fatigue after iron in women with low ferritin, and extend them by describing how the effect depends on dose. The pattern in ferritin, with smaller gains per milligram at the highest dose, fits absorption studies showing that larger doses raise hepcidin and lower the fraction absorbed. It is notable that fatigue continued to improve with dose even though the gain in ferritin per milligram became smaller, which suggests that the symptom may respond to the amount of iron absorbed rather than to the stores measured by ferritin.
The trial has several strengths. Allocation was concealed and participants and assessors were blinded, the capsules were identical in all arms, loss to follow-up was low, and the dose was modelled as a continuous variable, which uses all three arms to estimate a single slope. Fatigue was measured with a validated scale at four time points.
There are also limitations. The trial had no placebo arm, so the slope describes the difference between doses and not the effect of iron against none; part of the fall in fatigue in every arm may reflect regression to the mean or expectation. Most participants were young women, and the results may not apply to older adults, men or people with anaemia. Twelve weeks may be too short to see the full effect of the lower doses, which might catch up with longer treatment. Fatigue is self-reported and subjective, although the blinding reduces the risk that expectation differed between arms. Finally, we studied a single iron salt taken daily, and alternate-day dosing or other formulations may behave differently.
For practice, the results suggest that higher daily doses relieve fatigue more within this range, but the gain must be weighed against more frequent side effects, which may reduce adherence outside a trial. Future trials should include a placebo arm, test alternate-day schedules and follow participants for longer.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text: In iron-deficient, non-anaemic adults, the reduction in fatigue after 12 weeks of oral iron increased with the daily dose between 20 and 60 mg, while gastrointestinal adverse events also became more common. Dose choice should balance both effects.

alerts.description: An expression of concern was published for this paper.
A retraction notice was published for this paper.

documents.text:
Expression of concern: Dose-response of iron supplementation on fatigue

The editors have received concerns about the calculation of the dose-response analysis in this article and are investigating.

Retraction and replacement: Dose-response of iron supplementation on fatigue

Following the editors' investigation, this article is retracted and replaced by a corrected version (doi 10.9999/fake.2019.011v2). The dose-response slope in Table 3 was miscalculated: it was reported as 0.45 points per 10 mg and the correct value is 0.28 points per 10 mg. The finding that iron supplementation reduces fatigue is unchanged.

draft_doc.title: Iron and fatigue in student athletes
draft_doc.authors: Draft prepared for the Sports Nutrition Research Group, Fake College of Sport Science
draft_doc.abstract: Background: Student athletes combine heavy training with irregular meals and short sleep, and many report persistent tiredness. Low iron stores are one possible cause that can be treated. Aim: To estimate how the change in fatigue over a training term depends on the daily dose of oral iron in student athletes with low ferritin. Methods: An open-label, randomised dose-comparison study in student athletes with low ferritin, comparing two daily doses of oral iron over ten weeks of in-season training. Fatigue was measured with a 30-point self-report scale at the start and end of the term. Results and conclusions: Fatigue fell with increasing dose; the estimate, its interpretation and its comparison with earlier trials are given in the Results and Discussion.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Iron deficiency is common in athletes. Training increases iron losses through sweat, gastrointestinal bleeding and the breakdown of red cells in the soles of the feet during running, while exercise raises hepcidin for several hours and so reduces the absorption of dietary iron after a session [1, 2]. Female athletes, athletes on energy-restricted or vegetarian diets, and those who train at altitude are at particular risk [3, 4]. Surveys of university sports programmes have found low ferritin in a substantial share of athletes screened, most of whom had normal haemoglobin [5].
Tiredness is a frequent complaint among student athletes, who combine training with study, examinations and part-time work, and who often sleep less than they need [6, 8]. Distinguishing tiredness caused by low iron from the fatigue expected from training load is difficult, and the two may add to each other. Some athletes and coaches treat iron supplements as a general remedy for poor performance, taking high doses without testing, which risks side effects and, rarely, iron overload [9, 10].
Several trials in non-anaemic adults with low ferritin have found that oral iron reduces self-reported fatigue [11, 12], and studies in athletes have reported improvements in ferritin and, less consistently, in endurance performance [13, 14]. Few studies have examined fatigue in athletes as their main outcome, and almost none have compared doses. Because higher doses cause more gastrointestinal complaints, which matter to athletes during competition, knowing how much benefit each extra milligram brings would help team physicians choose a dose [15].
We therefore compared two daily doses of oral iron in student athletes with low ferritin during a competitive term, and estimated the change in fatigue per unit of dose.

sections.heading: 2. Methods
sections.text:
2.1 Design and participants
The study was an open-label, randomised comparison of two daily doses of oral iron over ten weeks, carried out in the sports medicine clinic of a university during the in-season term. Student athletes aged 18 to 26 years who competed for a university team in an endurance or team sport were invited at their pre-season medical screening. Eligible athletes had a serum ferritin below 35 µg/L and a haemoglobin within the reference range. We excluded athletes with a current injury that prevented training, a known cause of fatigue other than iron deficiency, a raised C-reactive protein at screening, or iron supplementation in the previous three months. All participants gave written consent, and the university research ethics committee approved the study.
2.2 Intervention
Participants were randomised by sealed envelopes to 30 or 60 mg of elemental iron daily as ferrous sulphate tablets, taken in the morning before breakfast. Team physicians and coaches were not told the allocation, but participants knew their dose because the tablets differed in size. Training load was set by each team's coaches and recorded weekly as session duration multiplied by rated perceived exertion [16].
2.3 Outcomes
The primary outcome was the change in fatigue from the start to the end of the term, measured with a 30-point self-report fatigue scale on which higher scores mean more fatigue [17]. Ferritin and haemoglobin were measured at the start and end of the term in morning samples taken at least 24 hours after the last training session, to limit the effect of exercise-induced inflammation on ferritin [18]. Adverse events were recorded at a mid-term visit and at the final visit.
2.4 Analysis
The change in fatigue was regressed on the daily dose, adjusting for baseline fatigue, sex and mean weekly training load. The dose-response slope was expressed as points of fatigue per 10 mg of daily iron, with a 95% confidence interval [19].

sections.heading: 3. Results
sections.text:
3.1 Participants
Sixty-four athletes with low ferritin were randomised, 32 to each dose, and 58 completed the term. Most were women, and the most common sports were middle-distance running, rowing and football. Baseline fatigue, ferritin and training load were similar in the two groups (Table 1).
3.2 Fatigue and iron status
Fatigue fell in both groups during the term, and the fall was larger with the higher dose. In the adjusted model, our estimated slope was 0.41 fatigue points per 10 mg of daily iron. Ferritin rose in both groups and more in the 60 mg group. Gastrointestinal complaints were more common at 60 mg, and two athletes in that group changed to taking the tablet in the evening because of nausea before morning training.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Change in fatigue score from the start to the end of the term in each dose group.

sections.heading: 4. Discussion
sections.text:
In student athletes with low ferritin, fatigue over a competitive term fell more with the higher daily dose of oral iron. Our estimated slope of 0.41 fatigue points per 10 mg of iron is close to that of Park and Singh [7] (0.45 per 10 mg), which supports the validity of our design. Ferritin rose more with the higher dose, and gastrointestinal complaints were more frequent, as in earlier studies of oral iron [20].
The athletes in our study differ from most trial populations in that their training load varies from week to week and itself causes fatigue. We adjusted for mean training load, but changes in training across the term, for example during examination periods or before major competitions, may have affected fatigue independently of iron. Because the study was open-label, athletes on the higher dose may have expected more benefit, which could inflate the difference between groups on a self-reported outcome [21].
Other limitations are the small sample, which gives an imprecise slope, the short follow-up, and the use of only two doses, which cannot show whether the effect levels off. Ferritin is raised by inflammation after heavy exercise, so even with the 24-hour rule some values may overstate iron stores [18]. We did not measure performance, and lower fatigue does not necessarily mean better results in competition.
For team physicians, the results suggest that the higher dose relieves fatigue more but at a cost in side effects that may matter before training or competition. Alternate-day dosing, which may improve absorption and reduce side effects, deserves testing in athletes [22]. A blinded trial with three or more doses and a longer follow-up would give a firmer estimate of the dose-response.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: In student athletes with low iron stores, a higher daily dose of oral iron was followed by a larger reduction in fatigue during a competitive term, with more gastrointestinal side effects. Screening and dose choice should take both into account.

expected.why: Rubric: a retraction and replacement where a corrected version exists = medium (not high); the later retraction supersedes the earlier concern, so relations is set. The draft only compares its own slope with the paper's: comparison x medium = low. The trap is the word 'retraction', which pulls models to high.
